questions.q: In the case study, what specifically is wrong with the pharmacy-benefits integration's setup?
options: It uses Per-User authentication instead of Named Principal
It uses Shield Platform Encryption incorrectly
It has no OAuth scope configured at all

It's scoped to `full` OAuth access and authenticates as a "System Administrator" profile, giving an external integration far more access than its actual job (reading benefits data) requires -- a severe least-privilege violation
questions.explain: The integration's `full` scope plus System Administrator profile gives it broad administrative capability far beyond what a benefits-data integration actually needs -- exactly the least-privilege violation Lesson 2 and Lesson 10 warn about.

questions.q: What specific failure pattern does the `MemberLookupService` class illustrate, and which lesson does it map to?
options: A `without sharing` class built for one legitimate internal purpose (batch job) later reused from an unrelated, member-facing context without anyone re-examining the sharing implications -- exactly Lesson 9's warning about sharing-bypass reuse
A SOQL injection vulnerability, mapping to Lesson 9's injection coverage
An encryption scheme mismatch, mapping to Lesson 7
A Health Check scoring problem, mapping to Lesson 11
questions.explain: This is a direct instance of Lesson 9's warning: a without-sharing class created for a legitimate reason (nightly batch job) gets reused later from a completely different context (member self-service portal) without anyone revisiting whether that sharing bypass still makes sense -- now potentially exposing other members' data.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the org's 68% Health Check score, while a real symptom, is an incomplete picture of the org's security problems?
options: Because Health Check scores are never accurate

Because Health Check measures org-wide settings like password policy, not things like the integration's OAuth scope/profile or the MemberLookupService sharing-bypass reuse, which require the fuller review checklist to catch
Because a 68% score actually indicates excellent security
Because Health Check only applies to orgs without any integrations
questions.explain: Consistent with Lesson 11, Health Check only scores org-wide settings such as password policy -- it has no visibility into integration scoping or custom Apex sharing behavior, both of which are serious problems in this case study that the score alone would miss.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about Setup Audit Trail being enabled but never reviewed in the case study org?
options: It means the org has strong monitoring in place, since the feature itself is active
It means Setup Audit Trail is a paid Shield feature that wasn't properly licensed
It's a layer that technically exists but provides essentially zero actual protection, because nothing reads it -- enabling a monitoring tool isn't the same as monitoring actually happening
It has no bearing on the org's overall security posture
questions.explain: A monitoring tool that's enabled but never reviewed provides no real detection capability -- consistent with Lesson 4's point that monitoring is a designed, acted-upon layer, not just a feature toggle.

questions.q: What is this case study's main point about how real security incidents typically happen?
options: They almost always result from one dramatic, novel attack technique nobody could have anticipated
They are primarily caused by Health Check scores below 50%
They only happen when Shield Platform Encryption is not purchased

They are usually combinations of multiple ordinary, individually explainable gaps (over-scoped integration, reused sharing bypass, unreviewed field access) that compound together, rather than one exotic failure
questions.explain: The lesson's explicit point is that every gap in the scenario is an ordinary, individually explainable instance of a concept already covered -- real incidents are usually combinations of ordinary gaps compounding, not one dramatic new attack type.
